items.title: Evan Christopher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 1, 2009
items.q: still getting thousands of dollars for their appearances: Hank Jones and Ornette

ctx.x: I think it’s a double edged sword to try to — look we’re in the period where there’s a level of alienation from the arts in general that’s high enough that I don’t think we need to make it worse by re-framing jazz or by continuing this track of framing it as a higher art. I mean I think all of it needs to be brought down through education, that’s how I would do it, to a level where the function of the music is not only more evident but viewed as essential. I think it’s not only jazz that needs to be returned to…

obligatory cultural experiences. But I think classical music needs to kind of have the same battle. I think especially when the economy is like this. You can’t continue to kind of act like the audience’s concerns aren’t important in a way, as if what you’re doing is so important that oh, they’ll come when they figure it out. You know I think we need to equally present ourselves as artists. Not just jazz, but I think we need to put ourselves on doorsteps for people and say here we are. Like we can help you. This…

Coleman. There’s a handful. But there’s not. So if you don’t have giants then you’ve got people that are just being marketed very well. And if that becomes sort of your top tier, and everybody else is kind of on the bottom, there’s this huge hole in the middle. There’s $5,000 and less, and $50,000 and more. But in between it’s a little tricky. And I don’t know if that was intentional.
